title: Votes of no confidence in Sinn Féin ministers fail
content_c:
Votes of no confidence in Sinn Féin ministers fail
- Published
Votes of no confidence in First Minister Michelle O'Neill and three other Sinn Féin ministers have fallen after failing to secure enough support in Stormont.
The Northern Ireland Assembly debated the no-confidence motions over the ministers' handling of the Drumcree dispute, after they received the backing of unionist parties last week.
However, the attempt to oust them failed as it required cross-community support from a majority of both unionists and nationalists in the assembly.
O'Neill described the move as "pointless" but Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said her power-sharing partner had "shattered" public confidence and needed to be held accountable.
It comes amid a major political row over a planned Orange Order march in Portadown, County Armagh.
O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin politicians have been heavily criticised by unionists for joining protests which have blocked the parade from passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road.
- What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? 
  - Published29 September
- Four key takeaways from the Drumcree dispute so far 
  - Published2 days ago
- First minister rejects call to resign over Drumcree row 
  - Published5 October
Police are investigating the demonstrations in a "large-scale" criminal inquiry.
The first minister again defended her involvement in blocking the Garvaghy Road during the debate, describing the planned Orange Order march as "triumphalist and sectarian".
Motions of no-confidence in the assembly are not binding without cross-community support from both unionist and nationalist MLAs, and cannot automatically force a minister from office.
Speaking during the assembly debate, Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) member Timothy Gaston, who tabled the no-confidence motions, described O'Neill as the "first minister of lawlessness" who "doesn't want an Orangeman about the place".
He asked: "If a determination can be set aside simply because republican protesters object to it, what confidence can any loyalist, any Orangeman, any unionist, have in the impartial administration of justice here in Northern Ireland?"
He said there needed to be "political consequences" for Sinn Féin and reiterated TUV's call for the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) to withdraw their deputy first minister to trigger the removal of O'Neill from the first minister post.
'Shattered'
Little-Pengelly said that people across Northern Ireland have been "appalled" by the conduct of Sinn Féin ministers.
"I would appeal to those sitting opposite to get a grip and realise that you have done damage," the DUP minister told the assembly.
"Damage to these institutions, damage to the ministerial roles that they should feel privileged to hold.
"That confidence from the people of Northern Ireland has been shattered."
O'Neill said it was "no surprise" unionist parties had supported the no-confidence motions because "they have never accepted equality".
"They have never accepted rights and respect, and again they still haven't respected the fact that it is now 2026."
The exclusion motions have also been submitted against John O'Dowd, Caoimhe Archibald and Liz Kimmins.
O'Dowd, who is also the finance minister, told the assembly he was "proud" to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents.
He accused the TUV of wanting to bring Stormont down.
Earlier, he told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme that he would continue to work with other parties.
"I am seeking engagements around the budget, I want to work with parties to make a better society for everyone."
Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald said the parading dispute had been used to create "instability" and said "the days of Orange domination are done".
Kimmins, who is the infrastructure minister, added that she had seen both "some of the most regressive elements of loyalism and unionism" over recent weeks and "the very best of our communities" in support of Garvaghy Road residents.
The motions gained the required 30 signatures with the backing of assembly members from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) and the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP).
Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme, the TUV leader, Jim Allister, admitted the debate was "not going to succeed succeed because of the absurd system whereby it needs cross-community support".
"But that accentuates the pressure on the DUP to be seen to do something because as things stand lawbreakers are sitting in our executive."
'Abject failure'
DUP assembly member Jonathan Buckley, who signed the no-confidence motions, accused Sinn Féin of "abject failure of political leadership".
"The genesis of today's debate may be about a parade, but it is about much more," he told the assembly.
"It is about the rule of law. It is about those who feel they are above it and not accountable to it".
Earlier, DUP leader Gavin Robinson called for sanctions to be introduced against anyone who broke the law.
Robinson said he plans to speak to the secretary of state on Monday evening to ensure that there is "accountability".
He said the legislation should be "brought forward that will bring sanctions so that anyone who has broken the law is subject to it and punished".
Regarding what actions the DUP could take, Robinson said "nothing is of the table".
The DUP and Ulster Unionists share power with Sinn Féin in a four-party devolved government alongside the Alliance Party.
Jim Allister has been urging the DUP to withdraw Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy first minister to trigger the removal of O'Neill as first minister.
Earlier on Good Morning Ulster, Robinson had said that he is "not in the territory" to "destabilise".
However his party colleague, Carla Lockhart, who represents the Upper Bann constituency in Westminster, said it "cannot be business as usual" at Stormont and the DUP has it "within its gift to remove" O'Neill from her position.
Robinson said that when the party comes to a "consensus, that is our position".
He added that Lockhart has "the right to stand up for her constituents".
UUP leader Jon Burrows called Sinn Féin "morally bankrupt" and said the party had "a recurring problem with accountability".
"We have a party that simply will not sign up to the normal rules of democracy," he told the assembly.
Addressing those on the Sinn Féin benches, Burrows said they should be "ashamed of their conduct".
Earlier, he told BBC Radio Ulster's Nolan Show he would not withdraw Health Minister Robbie Butler from the executive, "because to do so would affect the people of Northern Ireland in all the work he is doing".
Burrows said he was instead calling for changes to Stormont's rules, and said there should be "proper accountability mechanisms" to hold ministers who breach the pledge of office to account.
'Depressing, dispiriting'
Alliance Party deputy leader Eóin Tennyson branded the no-confidence motions a "political stunt" designed to collapse Stormont.
Tennyson described the debate as "depressing, dispiriting and almost unbelievable", warning that power-sharing institutions were "once again being placed in jeopardy".
However, he also said any elected representatives found to have acted unlawfully in recent weeks "should face the consequences of that conduct".
Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) assembly member Matthew O'Toole, leader of Stormont's official opposition, welcomed the NI Secretary's decision to ban the Drumcree parade, a dispute which he said had "opened up deep wounds that didn't need to be reopened".
O'Toole said he was not "diminishing or trivialising the rule of law" and his party would "cooperate" with investigations.
"Because we do accept the rule of law and the need for the PSNI and the courts to do their job," he added.
"But we were also founded, the SDLP, in the tradition of peaceful protest.
"That's in our DNA and that right is sacrosanct, and sometimes such action is unavoidable."

The motions gained the required 30 signatures with the backing of assembly members from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) and the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP).
Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme, the TUV leader, Jim Allister, admitted the debate was "not going to succeed succeed because of the absurd system whereby it needs cross-community support".
"But that accentuates the pressure on the DUP to be seen to do something because as things stand lawbreakers are sitting in our executive."
'Abject failure'
DUP assembly member Jonathan Buckley, who signed the no-confidence motions, accused Sinn Féin of "abject failure of political leadership".
"The genesis of today's debate may be about a parade, but it is about much more," he told the assembly.
"It is about the rule of law. It is about those who feel they are above it and not accountable to it".
Earlier, DUP leader Gavin Robinson called for sanctions to be introduced against anyone who broke the law.
Robinson said he plans to speak to the secretary of state on Monday evening to ensure that there is "accountability".
He said the legislation should be "brought forward that will bring sanctions so that anyone who has broken the law is subject to it and punished".
Regarding what actions the DUP could take, Robinson said "nothing is of the table".
The DUP and Ulster Unionists share power with Sinn Féin in a four-party devolved government alongside the Alliance Party.
Jim Allister has been urging the DUP to withdraw Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy first minister to trigger the removal of O'Neill as first minister.
Earlier on Good Morning Ulster, Robinson had said that he is "not in the territory" to "destabilise".
However his party colleague, Carla Lockhart, who represents the Upper Bann constituency in Westminster, said it "cannot be business as usual" at Stormont and the DUP has it "within its gift to remove" O'Neill from her position.
Robinson said that when the party comes to a "consensus, that is our position".
He added that Lockhart has "the right to stand up for her constituents".
UUP leader Jon Burrows called Sinn Féin "morally bankrupt" and said the party had "a recurring problem with accountability".
"We have a party that simply will not sign up to the normal rules of democracy," he told the assembly.
Addressing those on the Sinn Féin benches, Burrows said they should be "ashamed of their conduct".
Earlier, he told BBC Radio Ulster's Nolan Show he would not withdraw Health Minister Robbie Butler from the executive, "because to do so would affect the people of Northern Ireland in all the work he is doing".
Burrows said he was instead calling for changes to Stormont's rules, and said there should be "proper accountability mechanisms" to hold ministers who breach the pledge of office to account.
'Depressing, dispiriting'
Alliance Party deputy leader Eóin Tennyson branded the no-confidence motions a "political stunt" designed to collapse Stormont.
Tennyson described the debate as "depressing, dispiriting and almost unbelievable", warning that power-sharing institutions were "once again being placed in jeopardy".
However, he also said any elected representatives found to have acted unlawfully in recent weeks "should face the consequences of that conduct".
Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) assembly member Matthew O'Toole, leader of Stormont's official opposition, welcomed the NI Secretary's decision to ban the Drumcree parade, a dispute which he said had "opened up deep wounds that didn't need to be reopened".
O'Toole said he was not "diminishing or trivialising the rule of law" and his party would "cooperate" with investigations.
"Because we do accept the rule of law and the need for the PSNI and the courts to do their job," he added.
"But we were also founded, the SDLP, in the tradition of peaceful protest.
"That's in our DNA and that right is sacrosanct, and sometimes such action is unavoidable."

title: AI is less regulated than milk, says Microsoft president
content_c:
AI is less regulated than milk, says Microsoft president
- Published
Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said.
Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released.
His comments put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms don't lose out to Chinese rivals.
But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."
Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology is a threat to humanity.
The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown, but Trump has pushed against this.
Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Smith called AI both a "tool and a weapon" that urgently needed to be regulated.
"Let's get started today," he said.
He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way.
He also said there should be a legal requirement for firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue. He also suggested that independent government evaluators should vet new AI technology.
"We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI."
Smith said the UK was best placed to drive forward these global rules for AI because of its AI Security Institute, external, launched during former prime minister Rishi Sunak's government as the AI Safety Institute.
"In the world of technology, in the tech sector, most people that I know would say, if you ask them, name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it's very simple. It's the United Kingdom. They are the best."
'The moment has arrived'
Smith's views are very different to those of his president, who believes the US should be going full-steam ahead on AI.
Trump has repeatedly said that "whoever wins AI, wins".
However, Smith does not believe the US government would be as opposed to UK-led AI regulations as Trump's comments make it seem, suggesting the US would be more accepting of the UK making standards than the EU.
"In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels – that's a strength," he said.
"When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived.
"Let's speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together. I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country."
Big Boss Interview: Microsoft's Brad Smith
The president of the tech giant calls for global rules on AI, and says the UK is in the "best position" to lead the charge.
At the end of last month, Trump hosted the leaders of US tech giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta, and Google at the White House where the executives signed a "morally binding" document.
The companies agreed to work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and make sure they do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways".
Smith said he applauds the statement and Microsoft is "happy to sign it".
"It's a good step, it's a necessary step... But I don't think it's sufficient any longer."
He added that the challenge for any "self-regulatory regime" is that "the good companies will do what you want".
"It's the companies that are not as responsible that you need to worry about."

title: Australian politics live: Climate protester restrained after interrupting NSW parliament; Albanese says he’ll do whatever he can to stop ‘abhorrent’ US execution live stream
content_c:
Australian politics live: Climate protester restrained after interrupting NSW parliament; Albanese says he’ll do whatever he can to stop ‘abhorrent’ US execution live stream
Climate protester restrained by MPs after interrupting NSW parliament
Penry Buckley
A climate protester has been restrained by NSW MPs after he climbed over a barrier to interrupt question time to protest against the approval of the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) coalmine extension by the state’s Independent Planning Commission last month.
Earlier this afternoon, question time was interrupted for several minutes by the protest, during which eight activists from environmental advocacy group Rising Tide threw pages of government and academic climate reports into the chamber, including the Net Zero Commission’s report on coalmining emissions, which said mine expansions are against the state’s legislated emissions reduction targets.
In the parliamentary livestream, MPs appeared shocked before the speaker, Greg Piper, cut the feed. Footage shared by the group Rising Tide, which organised the protest, showed two MPs, independent MP Michael Regan and Labor MP David Saliba, helping parliamentary staff restrain one protester who climbed over the barrier.
In a statement, the protester, Andrew Sneddon, said he had been driven to do so by “the Minns government’s failure to address the climate crisis”.
We need a government that listens to its own experts, stops approving new fossil fuel projects and delivers an urgent, fair transition for coal workers and communities.
As the world hurtles towards climate catastrophe, we cannot stand by in silence. If our government won’t act with the urgency this crisis demands, everyday people like myself are forced to step up.
The Minns government has been contacted for comment.
Notorious childcare pedophile confronted in court as extradition to NSW to face 180 charges approved
One of Australia’s most notorious pedophiles has had abuse hurled at him in court after a move interstate to face 180 more charges was approved, AAP reports.
A victim supporter vented her fury at former childcare worker Ashley Paul Griffith, 48, in Brisbane magistrates court on Tuesday, screaming: “Rot! Rot! Fire! Brimstone! Burn!”.
Griffith was jailed for life with a non-parole period of 27 years in Queensland in November 2024 after pleading guilty to 307 child sexual offences.
He has also been charged in New South Wales with 180 child sexual offences allegedly committed against 23 girls at a childcare centre in Sydney between 2014 and 2017.
The victim supporter yelled “get fucked Ashley” and “disgusting piece of feral flesh” as Griffith was led from the court after the application for his transfer to NSW was granted by magistrate Belinda Merrin.
A thin Griffith wearing an ill-fitting green hooded jacket and thongs appeared impassive throughout the hearing.
The magistrate was told an application had been filed on 13 July on behalf of the NSW attorney general, Michael Daley.
That followed an application on 26 June by Queensland attorney general, Deb Frecklington, who had unsuccessfully asked for the transfer to be fast-tracked.
The application was not opposed by Griffith’s barrister Matt Black.
The path for Griffith to be transferred to face the NSW charges was cleared in June after his appeal against the severity of his Queensland sentence was dismissed.
Merrin did not specify a date or time for Griffith’s transfer.
Throughout two decades of preying on children in Queensland, Griffith filmed all but one of his victims, building a vast cache of abuse he shared online.
When detectives raided his Gold Coast home in 2022, they seized more than 4,000 child abuse images and videos documenting much of his offending.
The offences related to more than 60 victims aged between one and nine, including 28 rapes of preschool-aged girls in Queensland childcare centres.
The Northern Territory is set to legalise the use of OC Spray, citing a 99% success rate for its trial.
Availability will also be expanded, with 16 and 17-year-olds allowed to carry the spray with parental permission, the NT government said.
OC (oleoresin capsicum) spray is also know as pepper spray. It causes immediate inflammation and severe burning sensation in the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract.
“Territorians have embraced OC Spray for self-defence and made it clear they want to continue to have access and they want to see that access expanded to younger people,” chief minister Lia Finocchiaro said on Tuesday.
“During the trial, we had a lot of feedback about OC spray only being available to people aged 18 years and over, with many parents telling us that they wanted their 16 and 17-year-olds to have access as well.”
Eligible people aged 16 and 17 will be able to buy, possess, carry and use controlled OC spray, with consent required from parents or guardians who must not be prohibited persons.
Pepper spray provides a self defence option for young people, many of whom held down night-time jobs, Finocchiaro said.
“The reality is that we already give 16-year-olds a lot of responsibility – they can drive a car, many of them have jobs and parents want assurance that their children can defend themselves in a dangerous situation.”
Having access to OC spray could be the difference between life and death, or serious injury, the chief minister said.
A rigorous trial process had made sure police retained firm control over who had access to the spray, she told reporters in Darwin.
The new arrangements ban young people from taking OC spray into school grounds.
They also expand pepper spray use within NT households, allowing residents and eligible visitors to deploy it for self-defence in “genuine emergency situations”.
A husband for example would be able to buy OC spray for his wife and children aged 16 and above for self-defence in their home.
Availability will also be extended to roles in security, hospitality, crowd control and licensed venues.
Since the trial began, 5,976 OC spray canisters have been purchased in the territory.
Police have seized 69 canisters and identified 46 prohibited purchasers, representing 1.2% of buyers.
“It is a stunning result to have a 99% success rate with a reform of this magnitude,” Finocchiaro said.
“There’s no question in my mind that this is a safe, non-lethal ability for everyday Australians to protect themselves.”
Western Australia is the only other jurisdiction in the country allowing the general sale of OC spray.
Deputy opposition leader asked about MP’s ‘stoning’ comment
Back on Afternoon Briefing on the ABC, the deputy opposition leader, Ted O’Brien, is asked about comments from the member for Moncrieff, Angie Bell, who said in parliament the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and small business minister, Anne Aly, should be “shamed and stoned in the square” over the tax office’s decision to ban credit cards being used to pay tax bills.
Bell was forced to withdraw the comments, made on the floor of the House of Reps.
“Look, Angie was the first then to hop up and withdraw her comments,” O’Brien says, before pivoting to praising Bell’s willingness to “fight” for her electorate.
However, pushed by Patricia Karvelas, O’Brien concedes “tone and language” matter in politics.
“And that is why she did the right thing by withdrawing.”
One Nation treasury spokesperson, Barnaby Joyce, has challenged Jim Chalmers to a debate on the economy.
Speaking at Parliament House in Canberra, Joyce, who defected from the Nationals last year, says he has “a rough idea” what he’s doing in the portfolio.
“I’m happy to pull myself up against Chalmers any day of the week, if you want to line it up, I’ll have a lot of fun there,” he says.
He says he is happy to debate Tim Wilson, the shadow treasurer, as well, but concedes One Nation is “not out to kill the Coalition”.
“We’re out to get rid of the socialist government. We believe it’s a socialist government. I was thinking this morning … what happens if there wasn’t One Nation who weren’t doing the job we’re doing?
“Australia would be a very depressing place because you know you’re in the status quo. You know it’s stagnant.”
Worst conditions in Australia since the depression, Hanson says
Tom McIlroy
The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, says economic conditions in Australia are the worst since the Great Depression, including for business operators, the manufacturing sector and the homeless.
“I have never seen the country as bad as this, as what I am seeing at the moment,” she has told an Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry event in Canberra.
“Politics in Australia is changing. It’s changing because people have never done as tough as what they are now.
“I don’t think I remember a time, apart from the depression, that I have heard about, [with] the number of people who are homelesses in our country, the number of small businesses that have gone insolvent.”
A few more things from Anthony Albanese’s interview withPatricia Karvelas.
The prime minister confirms he will attend the Cop31 climate conference – Australia is joint host – in Turkey next month.
It’s been in my diary for some time.
I’ve been invited specifically by President Erdogan, the relationship with Turkey is a very important one.
And I think it sends a really good message that you essentially have leadership of this Cop from Turkey and Australia, two countries that are geographically very, very distant, have different economies, different cultures, but which are working together in the interests of humanity.
The PM is asked his opinion of the Trump administration considering livestreaming the execution by firing squad of former US soldier Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people in a mass shooting on a military base more than a decade ago.
Australia has had a bipartisan position of opposition to the death penalty. And I find the idea of livestreaming the death of anybody completely abhorrent. We should do whatever we can to stop that occurring.
I don’t know why anyone would want themselves to watch such an event, let alone sit back and allow potentially kids and families to get access to this.
Pauline Hanson is speaking at the same time as the PM.
The One Nation leader is attending a conference hosted by the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry at Parliament House.
She slams the Albanese government over its handling of the economy, including the Australian Taxation Office ban on credit cards and tough conditions for small business operators.
Hanson says she and One Nation’s treasury spokesperson, Barnaby Joyce, have experience running small businesses, something she says is in contrast with the Labor frontbench.
“One Nation wants Australia to be the best place in the world to do business,” Hanson says. “Not one of the best. The best.”
Hanson has called for government to get out of the way of business operators, to cut red tape and provide sustainable energy supply.
Albanese denies his government is in a ‘midterm slump’
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is appearing on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing program.
He is taken to comments he made to his own caucus that the government “would be kicking with the wind in the fourth quarter” (an Australian rules reference from a rugby league-following PM).
Albanese is asked whether this is a concession his government is in a “midterm slump”.
No, what it means is that you need to make sure that we continue to be focused on the needs of Australians.
We need to make sure as well that we’re focused on, where are we at, a year ahead, 10 years ahead.
How do we set Australia up for the stronger future?
Albanese also – uninvited – reflects on the former Kooyong MP Josh Frydenberg “stalking” the opposition leader, Angus Taylor. Frydenberg has published a book, seen as an undeclared, and as yet uncommitted – but still very public – consideration of a return to politics.
Detained democracy campaigner to meet consular officials in Vietnam
The detained Australian democracy campaigner Tran Hiep will be able to meet Australian consular officials in Vietnam for the first time since his sudden arrest nearly a month ago.
The 51-year-old hasn’t been directly heard from since before he failed to board his flight from the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh, on 18 September after meeting with human rights defenders.
Vietnamese authorities confirmed he had been arrested and charged with alleged terrorism and forging identity documents and it’s understood he is being held in Ho Chi Minh City’s B34 pre-trial detention centre.
Hiep’s wife, Chloe Dang, has told Guardian Australia he will soon be granted his first in-person visit with consular officials though contact with his family is still not allowed.
The Labor MP Emma Comergot booted, as did the Nationals MP Kevin Hogan, after he accused the government of running a “protection racket” around small business minister, Anne Aly.
Tony Burkewould not confirm whether the commonwealth would approve or reject a massive coalmine extension in NSW.
Some more from the NSW parliament, where the state government has introduced legislation to establish the Great Koala national park.
The member for the Blue Mountains, Trish Doyle, who introduced the bill said the state forests in the legislation would only be incorporated in the new park once the Clean Energy Regulator had formally recognised the associated carbon project.
Penny Sharpe said 13% of the 178,000 hectares would be designated regional reserve, rather than national park, to allow recreational activities such as bushwalking, trail-bike riding, camping and four-wheel driving to continue, as well as dog walking in select reserves. She said this decision followed community feedback.
The bill would allow the minister to approve motor racing events on existing regional roads in regional parks within the Great Koala national park, “recognising the long history of car rally events in the region”.
The government said it continued to support affected forestry workers, with the bill containing a provision enabling Forestry Corporation staff to be appointed to suitable roles within NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service.
NSW government introduces bill to establish Great Koala national park
The New South Wales government has introduced legislation to establish the long-promised Great Koala national park.
The new park will add more than 178,000 hectares of state forest to the national parks estate, with the government estimating it will protect 12,000 koalas, 36,000 gliders and more than 100 threatened species.
The park will go ahead after a contentious regulatory change by the Albanese government allowing state governments to earn carbon credits by storing carbon dioxide in native forests on public land.
Combined with existing national parks and reserves, it will be one of the largest parks in NSW, creating a protected area spanning more than 475,000 hectares.
The NSW environment minister, Penny Sharpe, said:
The Great Koala national park is one of the most important things we can do to save koalas in NSW. It is also about creating an area that people can explore and enjoy for generations.
State parliament will debate the bill next week and the government hopes the park will be officially gazetted and opened by the end of the year.
Government pay offer falls short, public service union says
The main public sector union says the federal government’s offer of a 9% pay rise over the next three years falls short of expectations.
The Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) put a 5% pay rise each year or equal to CPI – whichever is higher – which it said had been endorsed by more than 18,000 members.
The CPSU’s newly elected national secretary, Rebecca Fawcett, said the union would speak with members once more about next steps.
CPSU members [have] been clear from the beginning of these negotiations: they want to see pay that keeps up with the cost of living, which recognises the essential work they do every day. The APS-wide pay offer that has been tabled today falls short of what our members asked for, and what public sector workers deserve. This is now in our members’ hands. They will decide whether it is good enough, and the union will continue to fight for a pay offer that respects these vital workers, and the important services they deliver to the community.

“Territorians have embraced OC Spray for self-defence and made it clear they want to continue to have access and they want to see that access expanded to younger people,” chief minister Lia Finocchiaro said on Tuesday.
“During the trial, we had a lot of feedback about OC spray only being available to people aged 18 years and over, with many parents telling us that they wanted their 16 and 17-year-olds to have access as well.”
Eligible people aged 16 and 17 will be able to buy, possess, carry and use controlled OC spray, with consent required from parents or guardians who must not be prohibited persons.
Pepper spray provides a self defence option for young people, many of whom held down night-time jobs, Finocchiaro said.
“The reality is that we already give 16-year-olds a lot of responsibility – they can drive a car, many of them have jobs and parents want assurance that their children can defend themselves in a dangerous situation.”
Having access to OC spray could be the difference between life and death, or serious injury, the chief minister said.
A rigorous trial process had made sure police retained firm control over who had access to the spray, she told reporters in Darwin.
The new arrangements ban young people from taking OC spray into school grounds.
They also expand pepper spray use within NT households, allowing residents and eligible visitors to deploy it for self-defence in “genuine emergency situations”.
A husband for example would be able to buy OC spray for his wife and children aged 16 and above for self-defence in their home.
Availability will also be extended to roles in security, hospitality, crowd control and licensed venues.
Since the trial began, 5,976 OC spray canisters have been purchased in the territory.
Police have seized 69 canisters and identified 46 prohibited purchasers, representing 1.2% of buyers.
“It is a stunning result to have a 99% success rate with a reform of this magnitude,” Finocchiaro said.
“There’s no question in my mind that this is a safe, non-lethal ability for everyday Australians to protect themselves.”
Western Australia is the only other jurisdiction in the country allowing the general sale of OC spray.
Deputy opposition leader asked about MP’s ‘stoning’ comment
Back on Afternoon Briefing on the ABC, the deputy opposition leader, Ted O’Brien, is asked about comments from the member for Moncrieff, Angie Bell, who said in parliament the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and small business minister, Anne Aly, should be “shamed and stoned in the square” over the tax office’s decision to ban credit cards being used to pay tax bills.
Bell was forced to withdraw the comments, made on the floor of the House of Reps.
“Look, Angie was the first then to hop up and withdraw her comments,” O’Brien says, before pivoting to praising Bell’s willingness to “fight” for her electorate.
However, pushed by Patricia Karvelas, O’Brien concedes “tone and language” matter in politics.
“And that is why she did the right thing by withdrawing.”
One Nation treasury spokesperson, Barnaby Joyce, has challenged Jim Chalmers to a debate on the economy.
Speaking at Parliament House in Canberra, Joyce, who defected from the Nationals last year, says he has “a rough idea” what he’s doing in the portfolio.
“I’m happy to pull myself up against Chalmers any day of the week, if you want to line it up, I’ll have a lot of fun there,” he says.
He says he is happy to debate Tim Wilson, the shadow treasurer, as well, but concedes One Nation is “not out to kill the Coalition”.
“We’re out to get rid of the socialist government. We believe it’s a socialist government. I was thinking this morning … what happens if there wasn’t One Nation who weren’t doing the job we’re doing?
“Australia would be a very depressing place because you know you’re in the status quo. You know it’s stagnant.”
Worst conditions in Australia since the depression, Hanson says
Tom McIlroy
The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, says economic conditions in Australia are the worst since the Great Depression, including for business operators, the manufacturing sector and the homeless.
“I have never seen the country as bad as this, as what I am seeing at the moment,” she has told an Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry event in Canberra.
“Politics in Australia is changing. It’s changing because people have never done as tough as what they are now.
“I don’t think I remember a time, apart from the depression, that I have heard about, [with] the number of people who are homelesses in our country, the number of small businesses that have gone insolvent.”
A few more things from Anthony Albanese’s interview withPatricia Karvelas.
The prime minister confirms he will attend the Cop31 climate conference – Australia is joint host – in Turkey next month.
It’s been in my diary for some time.
I’ve been invited specifically by President Erdogan, the relationship with Turkey is a very important one.
And I think it sends a really good message that you essentially have leadership of this Cop from Turkey and Australia, two countries that are geographically very, very distant, have different economies, different cultures, but which are working together in the interests of humanity.
The PM is asked his opinion of the Trump administration considering livestreaming the execution by firing squad of former US soldier Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people in a mass shooting on a military base more than a decade ago.
Australia has had a bipartisan position of opposition to the death penalty. And I find the idea of livestreaming the death of anybody completely abhorrent. We should do whatever we can to stop that occurring.
I don’t know why anyone would want themselves to watch such an event, let alone sit back and allow potentially kids and families to get access to this.
Pauline Hanson is speaking at the same time as the PM.
The One Nation leader is attending a conference hosted by the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry at Parliament House.
She slams the Albanese government over its handling of the economy, including the Australian Taxation Office ban on credit cards and tough conditions for small business operators.
Hanson says she and One Nation’s treasury spokesperson, Barnaby Joyce, have experience running small businesses, something she says is in contrast with the Labor frontbench.
“One Nation wants Australia to be the best place in the world to do business,” Hanson says. “Not one of the best. The best.”
Hanson has called for government to get out of the way of business operators, to cut red tape and provide sustainable energy supply.
Albanese denies his government is in a ‘midterm slump’
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is appearing on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing program.
He is taken to comments he made to his own caucus that the government “would be kicking with the wind in the fourth quarter” (an Australian rules reference from a rugby league-following PM).
Albanese is asked whether this is a concession his government is in a “midterm slump”.
No, what it means is that you need to make sure that we continue to be focused on the needs of Australians.
We need to make sure as well that we’re focused on, where are we at, a year ahead, 10 years ahead.
How do we set Australia up for the stronger future?
Albanese also – uninvited – reflects on the former Kooyong MP Josh Frydenberg “stalking” the opposition leader, Angus Taylor. Frydenberg has published a book, seen as an undeclared, and as yet uncommitted – but still very public – consideration of a return to politics.
Detained democracy campaigner to meet consular officials in Vietnam
The detained Australian democracy campaigner Tran Hiep will be able to meet Australian consular officials in Vietnam for the first time since his sudden arrest nearly a month ago.
The 51-year-old hasn’t been directly heard from since before he failed to board his flight from the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh, on 18 September after meeting with human rights defenders.
Vietnamese authorities confirmed he had been arrested and charged with alleged terrorism and forging identity documents and it’s understood he is being held in Ho Chi Minh City’s B34 pre-trial detention centre.
Hiep’s wife, Chloe Dang, has told Guardian Australia he will soon be granted his first in-person visit with consular officials though contact with his family is still not allowed.
The Labor MP Emma Comergot booted, as did the Nationals MP Kevin Hogan, after he accused the government of running a “protection racket” around small business minister, Anne Aly.
Tony Burkewould not confirm whether the commonwealth would approve or reject a massive coalmine extension in NSW.
Some more from the NSW parliament, where the state government has introduced legislation to establish the Great Koala national park.
The member for the Blue Mountains, Trish Doyle, who introduced the bill said the state forests in the legislation would only be incorporated in the new park once the Clean Energy Regulator had formally recognised the associated carbon project.
Penny Sharpe said 13% of the 178,000 hectares would be designated regional reserve, rather than national park, to allow recreational activities such as bushwalking, trail-bike riding, camping and four-wheel driving to continue, as well as dog walking in select reserves. She said this decision followed community feedback.
The bill would allow the minister to approve motor racing events on existing regional roads in regional parks within the Great Koala national park, “recognising the long history of car rally events in the region”.
The government said it continued to support affected forestry workers, with the bill containing a provision enabling Forestry Corporation staff to be appointed to suitable roles within NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service.
NSW government introduces bill to establish Great Koala national park
The New South Wales government has introduced legislation to establish the long-promised Great Koala national park.
The new park will add more than 178,000 hectares of state forest to the national parks estate, with the government estimating it will protect 12,000 koalas, 36,000 gliders and more than 100 threatened species.
The park will go ahead after a contentious regulatory change by the Albanese government allowing state governments to earn carbon credits by storing carbon dioxide in native forests on public land.
Combined with existing national parks and reserves, it will be one of the largest parks in NSW, creating a protected area spanning more than 475,000 hectares.
The NSW environment minister, Penny Sharpe, said:
The Great Koala national park is one of the most important things we can do to save koalas in NSW. It is also about creating an area that people can explore and enjoy for generations.
State parliament will debate the bill next week and the government hopes the park will be officially gazetted and opened by the end of the year.
Government pay offer falls short, public service union says
The main public sector union says the federal government’s offer of a 9% pay rise over the next three years falls short of expectations.
The Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) put a 5% pay rise each year or equal to CPI – whichever is higher – which it said had been endorsed by more than 18,000 members.
The CPSU’s newly elected national secretary, Rebecca Fawcett, said the union would speak with members once more about next steps.
CPSU members [have] been clear from the beginning of these negotiations: they want to see pay that keeps up with the cost of living, which recognises the essential work they do every day. The APS-wide pay offer that has been tabled today falls short of what our members asked for, and what public sector workers deserve. This is now in our members’ hands. They will decide whether it is good enough, and the union will continue to fight for a pay offer that respects these vital workers, and the important services they deliver to the community.
Climate protester restrained by MPs after interrupting NSW parliament
Penry Buckley
A climate protester has been restrained by NSW MPs after he climbed over a barrier to interrupt question time to protest against the approval of the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) coalmine extension by the state’s Independent Planning Commission last month.
Earlier this afternoon, question time was interrupted for several minutes by the protest, during which eight activists from environmental advocacy group Rising Tide threw pages of government and academic climate reports into the chamber, including the Net Zero Commission’s report on coalmining emissions, which said mine expansions are against the state’s legislated emissions reduction targets.
In the parliamentary livestream, MPs appeared shocked before the speaker, Greg Piper, cut the feed. Footage shared by the group Rising Tide, which organised the protest, showed two MPs, independent MP Michael Regan and Labor MP David Saliba, helping parliamentary staff restrain one protester who climbed over the barrier.
In a statement, the protester, Andrew Sneddon, said he had been driven to do so by “the Minns government’s failure to address the climate crisis”.
We need a government that listens to its own experts, stops approving new fossil fuel projects and delivers an urgent, fair transition for coal workers and communities.
As the world hurtles towards climate catastrophe, we cannot stand by in silence. If our government won’t act with the urgency this crisis demands, everyday people like myself are forced to step up.
The Minns government has been contacted for comment.

title: Reform’s Zia Yusuf is sounding more and more like Trump every day | Zoe Williams
content_c:
Had Reform merely announced its intention to suspend the asylum system for an entire parliamentary term, I’d have just ignored it. Even to dignify its policy platform with a response is to enter its alternate universe, in which it’s preparing for government. I prefer, if only fractionally, this universe we’re in, where the party hangs by a thread on the results of a parliamentary inquiry into Nigel Farage’s £5m gift from a disinterested well-wisher.
Had Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, gone on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme merely promising a British version of ICE, I still would have ignored it, not due to complacency, more due to a bone-penetrating despair that anyone, even he, would look at the US’s shadow militia, performing staged acts of unfettered violence and inhumanity, and think: “That looks cool – I bet I could get some political capital out of that.”
However, as Yusuf laid out his arguments, they were so dumb, so random, disconnected, hammy and cliche-riddled, just so unremittingly stupid, that it turned out to be impossible not to react. I cannot let his nonsense slide. It would be an insult to words.
An elderly woman, he said, waited 23 hours for an ambulance and the coroner found this contributed to her death. A Welsh 15-year-old’s educational attainment is below the OECD average. Many young people have to live with their parents into their 30s and 40s because they can’t afford rent. How does any of this relate to asylum seekers? Are they displacing elderly people in ambulance-demand? It seems unlikely, although if they are an immediate fix would be to stop masked gangs surrounding their living quarters and scaring the hell out of them. Those are ethno-nationalist thugs, of course, and nothing to do with Reform.
High private rents, meanwhile, are not driven by asylum seekers, who have no right to work even if they arrive through a formal route, and as for Welsh 15-year-olds … well, we have some data here. They’re underperforming compared with English 15-year-olds, who are above the OECD average, indeed, above every other European nation, except Estonia and Ireland. If migrants destroy educational standards, how is Ireland managing to thrive? Why, with its very low number of asylum seekers, is Slovenia full of 15-year-olds who (no offence) suck at reading?
None of it makes sense because none of it was meant to. It’s bilge punctuated by soothing mantras (“Charity begins at home”, Yusuf repeated), aimed at the half-asleep mind dreaming of a whites-only yesteryear. It had that in common with a Trump rally, but lacked his pizzazz. Reform can’t even do neo-fascist mimicry right.
A word entered my social-media lexicon recently, which I wish I’d never had cause to look up, because I wish it wasn’t so useful: “agnotology” is the deliberate creation of ignorance, confusion and doubt. You can do it with misinformation and fake news, or you can do it with half-truths pouring out of bot factories, then leave an entire body politic tearing chunks out of itself as it seeks to establish whether the discursive environment has been deliberately polluted, or whether people are just mean and wrong nowadays. But you can also do it by simply talking nonsense, which we’ve seen writ large in party conference season and its aftermath.
“Let’s build an impenetrable and state-of-the-art defence dome for £10bn, and call it the Britannia Shield, even though that’s already the name of a Oxfordshire roofing company,” says the party that spent vastly more than that trying and failing to build the HS2 train line. “Let’s stop all refugees coming from everywhere, until the conditions for every single Briton at every conceivable stage of life have been improved,” from the party whose only discernible allegiance is to its billionaire donors.
The policies don’t even matter. Florid, premeditated stupidity is an end in itself, to clog the collective consciousness with nonsense, chase down every citizen who woke up in a good mood, with a scintilla of confidence about the future, and kill their mojo. The only defence is to hold your line. Insist on the difference between truth and untruth; guard your precious mojo with everything you’ve got.
Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

title: Germany: Labor Minister's resignation puts a spotlight on cracks within the government
content_c:
Germany: Labor Minister's resignation leaves the government in turmoil
October 12, 2026
The week kicked off with a bang: On Monday morning, Bärbel Bas announced her resignation as Labor Minister and as Co-Chair of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD). "Following the death of my stepdaughter, I realized that I need time to come to terms with my grief," Bärbel Bas wrote in a personal statement to party members.
However, she also cited "the public attacks against me — unfortunately, including some from within the ranks of our coalition partner" as reasons for her resignation. In fact, the pressure on Bas increased significantly in recent days. The centrist coalition government is urgently awaiting key legislative proposals from the Ministry of Labor.
Before the summer recess in July, a commission had already presented comprehensive proposals for reforming Germany's statutory pension system. The coalition partners of SPD and the center-right Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) wanted these proposals to be quickly turned into legislation. To date, however, no finalized drafts have been presented.
There had been calls for Bas' resignation
"The minister is no longer tenable. For months, she has been blocking the reforms our country so urgently needs," railed Christian von Stetten, head of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group's caucus representing medium-sized enterprises, said in reference to Bas in September.
In early October, such criticism was echoed by CDU Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, who demanded that the pension reform be passed by the end of the year. Bas had to submit the bill "promptly," Reiche said, although it was known at the time what a difficult personal situation her cabinet colleague was in at the time.
SPD co-leader, Finance Minister and Vice-Chancellor Lars Klingbeil reacted sharply on Monday, saying the political attacks against Bas had been "disgraceful." Following a meeting of the SPD leadership, he told journalists in Berlin: "This poisons the political discourse, and — in the interest of preserving our political culture — I hope that everyone will take a step back and reflect on what has actually happened over the past few weeks." He called on all centrist politicians to be careful "that we don't destroy the good people in politics by attacking one another."
Such accusations carry significant weight at a time when the coalition is already mired in a deep crisis.
Adding to this is the new vacancy at the top of the SPD. Without Bas, Klingbeil will lead the SPD alone. A party convention will be scheduled for December or January to elect new leadership for the Social Democrats. It is not certain whether Klingbeil will run again. He received a very poor result during his last reelection as party leader.
Swift replacement of Labor Minister
Alexander Schweitzer is to succeed Bärbel Bas as Federal Minister of Labor. The former state premier of the state of Rhineland-Palatinate had previously served as that state's Minister of Labor and Social Affairs. Chancellor Friedrich Merz expressed confidence that Schweitzer's experience would ensure " good cooperation within the federal government," adding that he hoped that the pending legislative proposals "will now be quickly approved by the cabinet and can be introduced into the parliamentary process."
The chancellor refuted the accusations leveled by Bas, saying that he had never discussed personal matters with her. Friedrich Merz said he had explicitly advised Bas to take the time she needed to grieve.
Merz promises change
Mistrust between the coalition partners has increased significantly, with SPD lawmakers speaking of an increasingly toxic political climate.
For months, the CDU and SPD have been grappling with low poll numbers, disappointing election results, and disputes over key reform projects. Plans for changes to the electricity tax, the introduction of a sugar tax, the pension and the labor market reform — hardly any initiative has been able to proceed without public controversy.
Adding to this is the crisis within the chancellor's party, the CDU, which saw a historic election defeat in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in September, when it even lost representation in a state parliament for the first time in history.
On Sunday and Monday, the party leadership met for a closed-door session to discuss the way forward.
They produced a four-page document which indicated a shift in priorities, putting more emphasis on social issues: affordable housing, lower electricity prices, better health care, and greater respect for citizens' lifetime achievements are mentioned in the paper. This is seen as a response to criticism that the CDU had been focusing too much on economic and regulatory issues.
The chancellor admitted that voters feel that politicians are not taking their hardships and fears of social decline seriously enough. "We have to work our way out of this slump — and get out of a crisis of confidence," Merz said. "You can't just reinvent a party overnight over a weekend, but we want to show that we're ready for change... and we have to be, given the election results."
The chancellor announced that he would lower the electricity tax for everyone — a promise he had made before the general election in 2025 but had not kept.
With the closed-door meeting paper, the CDU is also sending a signal to the SPD. Instead of a programmatic shift further to the right, it is emphasizing its traditional social values — a stance that resonates well within the Social Democrats.
The chancellor made an effort to emphasize his intention to continue with the current coalition government: "The personnel changes will not call into question the basis of the coalition agreement." He then repeated what he had recently said during a visit to Ukraine: "We need a stable federal government right now in order to remain capable of acting on the international stage."
Both CDU/CSU and SPD know that calling early elections could primarily benefit the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is leading in the polls nationwide. So despite the deep rifts, Klingbeil and Merz currently see no alternative to their coalition.
This article was originally published in German.

title: Bulgarien bittet EU und Nato nach Drohnenangriffen um Hilfe
content_c:
Attacke im Schwarzen Meer Bulgarien bittet EU und Nato nach Drohnenangriffen um Hilfe
Eine Woche nach Drohnenangriffen auf zwei Handelsschiffe im Schwarzen Meer hat Bulgarien die Europäische Union und die Nato um technische Hilfe bei den Ermittlungen gebeten. Beide angegriffenen Schiffe waren beschädigt worden, eines davon sank. Nach Angaben von Regierungschef Rumen Radew ist bislang unklar, ob die Drohnen aus Russland oder aus der Ukraine kamen.
Fest steht, dass eines der angegriffenen Schiffe, die »Alfa Watan«, praktisch sofort nach der Attacke gesunken war – binnen etwa drei Minuten. Eine Drohne, die derart enorme Schäden anrichtet, dürfte mit einem Sprengkopf von mehr als 300 Kilogramm ausgestattet gewesen sein, sagte der Professor an der Militärakademie in Sofia, Dimitar Nedjalkow, dem bulgarischen Fernsehsender Nova. An Bord der unter der Flagge von Togo fahrenden »Alfa Watan« waren zwölf Mann Besatzung, die noch immer vermisst werden.
Das zweite Schiff, die »Able«, war unter der Flagge von Palau mit Getreide nach Istanbul in der Türkei unterwegs, als es nach einem Drohnenangriff in Brand geriet. Die 18-köpfige Crew wurde gerettet. Auf dem Schiff wurden ersten Ermittlungen zufolge keine Drohnen-Reste entdeckt. Medienberichten zufolge hat die »Able« Bulgariens Gewässer inzwischen wieder verlassen.
Selenskyj macht Moskau für Angriffe verantwortlich
Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj sah in den Angriffen »einen weiteren Ausdruck der russischen Bemühungen, den westlichen Teil des Schwarzen Meeres für die Schifffahrt völlig untauglich zu machen«. Nach Kontakten mit der bulgarischen Seite sei festgestellt worden, »dass es sich um einen kombinierten russischen Angriff mit See- und Luftdrohnen handelt«.
description: Im Schwarzen Meer werden zwei Schiffe angegriffen, eines sinkt, die Besatzung verschwindet. Die Ukraine macht Russland für den Angriff verantwortlich – nun bittet Bulgarien um verstärkte Ermittlungshilfe.

title: Rücktritt von Bärbel Bas: Neue Hoffnung für Koalition?
content_c:
Rücktritt von Bärbel Bas Neue Hoffnung für die Koalition?
Ist der Rücktritt von Bärbel Bas eine Chance für einen Neuanfang in der Koalition? Kanzler Merz verspricht sich einiges vom neuen Arbeitsminister Schweitzer - doch sicher ist nichts im politischen Berlin.
Friedrich Merz spulte bei seinem ersten öffentlichen Auftritt nach der Rücktrittsankündigung von Bärbel Bas das Pflichtprogramm ab. Er "bedauere die persönliche Entscheidung, aber ich respektiere sie selbstverständlich", sagte der Kanzler auf einer Pressekonferenz in der CDU-Parteizentrale.
Er und "Frau Bas" hätten in den vergangenen eineinhalb Jahren "sehr gut und vertrauensvoll" zusammengearbeitet. Er habe ihr auch schon "persönlich seine guten Wünsche übermittelt und auch mein Mitgefühl für den Verlust in ihrer Familie", so Merz.
Bas trauert um ihre verstorbene Stieftochter und hatte in den vergangenen Wochen ihre politischen Termine zurückgefahren beziehungsweise komplett abgesagt, um sich um ihre familiären Angelegenheiten kümmern zu können.
Merz wirklich zufrieden gewesen?
Mitgefühl hat im politischen Geschäft - gerade in der Hauptstadt - aber eine kurze Halbwertzeit. Denn wenig später ließ der CDU-Kanzler auf der Pressekonferenz durchblicken, dass die Zusammenarbeit mit der Arbeits- und Sozialministerin von der SPD wohl nicht immer "sehr gut" gewesen ist, wie zuvor dargestellt.
Als Merz nämlich über ihren Nachfolger sprach: Alexander Schweitzer, ehemaliger Ministerpräsident von Rheinland-Pfalz. Der übernehme eine sehr große Verantwortung und "offene Gesetzgebungsvorhaben, von denen ich hoffe, dass sie jetzt schnell im Kabinett verabschiedet und in den parlamentarischen Prozess eingebracht werden können", sagte der Regierungschef der schwarz-roten Koalition. Eine höfliche Umschreibung in "Merz-Sprech" für: Ich erwarte, dass das Riesenministerium Arbeit und Soziales endlich liefert!
Bas wurde von Union kritisiert
Seit Monaten war von Unions-Politikern zu hören, Bas blockiere beschlossene Reformvorhaben: bei der Rente, bei der Flexibilisierung der Arbeitszeit, bei der Grundsicherung.
Die härteste Kritik kam von Christian von Stetten (CDU), dem Vorsitzenden des einflussreichen Parlamentskreises Mittelstand (PKM) der Unions-Fraktion. Bas sei als Ministerin "nicht mehr tragbar", hatte Christian von Stetten in einem Interview gesagt und damit für böses Blut in der Koalition gesorgt.
SPD-Chef Lars Klingbeil wies die Kritik an der Amtsführung von Bas am Abend zurück. Bas habe nicht gebremst. "Wir waren wie verabredet im Zeitplan, auch für die Rentenreform", sagte Klingbeil im ARD-Brennpunkt. Vielmehr habe es in der Koalition eine Verabredung gegeben, erst die drei Landtagswahlen in Sachsen-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern und Berlin abzuwarten, bevor Gesetze vorgelegt werden.
Schweitzer - nächste "Bremse" für Merz?
Der Kanzler pocht darauf, dass der verabredete Zeitplan für die Reformen eingehalten wird. Durch den Ministerwechsel "sollte es eher eine Beschleunigung der Prozesse geben", sagte Merz nach dem Rücktritt von Bas. Aber steht Alexander Schweitzer, der "Neue" an der Spitze des wichtigen Ministeriums, tatsächlich für die von Merz gewünschte Beschleunigung?
Schweitzer gilt beispielsweise als ausgewiesener Gegner der Abschaffung der abschlagsfreien Rente nach 45 Beitragsjahren ("Rente mit 63"). Als Schweitzer - der auch einer der stellvertretenden Bundesvorsitzenden der SPD ist - gestern das Willy-Brandt-Haus verließ, wollte er sich noch nicht zu seiner neuen Aufgabe in Berlin äußern. Er "sei rein privat hier", sagte er beim Rausgehen wartenden Journalisten.
Schweitzer ehrgeizig - und fachlich nah dran
Möglicherweise sagt Schweitzer heute etwas. Am Nachmittag überreicht Bundespräsident Frank-Walter Steinmeier dem neuen Arbeits- und Sozialminister seine Erkennungsurkunde. Auch ein erstes Gespräch mit dem Kanzler ist geplant, kündigte Lars Klingbeil in der ARD an. Schweitzer wolle "jetzt richtig starten und Dinge auf den Weg bringen", so Klingbeil über seinen Parteigenossen.
Der 53-jährige Jurist - Sohn eines Binnenschiffers - gilt als überaus ehrgeizig und ist im Stoff. Vor seiner Zeit als Regierungschef in Rheinland-Pfalz war Schweitzer dort Landesminister für Arbeit und Soziales.
Wie geht es weiter für Klingbeil?
Fraglich ist aber, wie es mit Finanzminister und Vizekanzler Lars Klingbeil weitergeht. Nach dem Rücktritt seiner Co-Vorsitzenden Bärbel Bas hatte Klingbeil angekündigt, dass die gesamte SPD-Führung neu gewählt werden soll. Dafür ist ein Parteitag zum Jahreswechsel geplant. Es ist offen, ob Klingbeil dort erneut für einen Platz in der Doppelspitze antritt.
Klingbeil ist intern nicht unumstritten. Bei seiner letzten Wiederwahl als Parteichef 2025 erhielt er nur rund 65 Prozent der Stimmen. Eine Klatsche, die bis heute nachwirkt. "Ich klebe nicht an meinem Amt", sagte Klingbeil im ARD-Brennpunkt. Er glaube aber, dass er der Partei und dem Land in einer schwierigen Phase helfen könne. "Aber darüber werden wir jetzt gemeinsam entscheiden", so Klingbeil weiter.
Klingbeil: "SPD steht zu dieser Regierung"
Die ungeklärte Machtfrage in der SPD könnte für die schwarz-rote Bundesregierung in den kommenden Wochen und Monaten zu einem Risiko werden. Wer führt die Sozialdemokraten in der Zukunft? Wer gibt bei ihnen künftig den Ton an im Koalitionsausschuss, wo die wichtigen Entscheidungen fallen?
Alles unklar. "Klar ist: Die SPD ist handlungsfähig. Die SPD steht zu dieser Regierung", so Klingbeil am Vormittag bei seinem Statement nach Bas‘ Rückzugsankündigung. Im politischen Geschäft hat allerdings nicht nur Mitgefühl eine geringe Halbwertzeit. Zusagen haben es auch.

title: Klimaziel: Deutschland muss Billionen investieren
content_c:
Klimaziel: Deutschland muss Billionen investieren
12. Oktober 2026
Laut der Studie des Prognos-Forschungsinstituts im Auftrag der Förderbank KfW müssen sich damit die bisherigen Ausgaben für den Klimaschutz mehr als verdoppeln. Den Großteil der Investitionen müssten demnach Verbraucher und Unternehmen stemmen, auf den Staat entfielen nur zwölf Prozent.
Beim Blick auf die Zahlen ist aber wichtig: Nur knapp die Hälfte aller Investitionen fiele zusätzlich an, weil auch dann Geld ausgeben würde, wenn man weiter auf fossile Energieträger wie Kohle, Öl und Gas setzen würde. "Der Betrag relativiert sich dadurch, dass Deutschland auch beim Festhalten an fossilen Technologien stark investieren müsste", erklärte KfW-Vorstandschef Stefan Wintels.
Von den zur Zielerreichung nötigen Investitionen von ungefähr 290 Milliarden Euro pro Jahr blieben also netto noch rund 145 Milliarden Euro übrig. Das ist der Teil, der durch die Umstellung auf mehr Klimaschutz hinzukommt.
Klimaziel ist gesetzlich festgeschrieben
Bis 2045 will Deutschland klimaneutral sein, also nicht mehr Treibhausgase ausstoßen, als wieder gespeichert werden können. Das ist gesetzlich festgeschrieben.
Die höchsten Ausgaben entfallen auf den Verkehrssektor, der fast die Hälfte ausmacht. Hier geht es vor allem um die Anschaffung von Pkw mit klimafreundlicheren Antrieben. Da aber ohnehin Autos gekauft würden und der Preisunterschied zwischen Elektroautos und Wagen mit Verbrennungsmotor schrumpft, müssten die Investitionen netto nur um ein knappes Fünftel steigen.
Ein Viertel der sechs Billionen Euro fällt im Energiesektor an. Hier sind die Nettoinvestitionen besonders groß, weil das Energiesystem komplett umgebaut werden müsste, wenn Strom aus Wind und Sonne eine größere Rolle spielt. Insbesondere in die Stromnetze muss dann Geld fließen. Hier sind besonders viele staatliche Investitionen nötig.
Rund ein Fünftel macht der Gebäudesektor aus, und zwar vor allem Wohngebäude. Hier sind laut Studie die meisten Extra-Investitionen nötig, also Ausgaben, die ohne mehr Klimaschutz nicht anfallen würden.
Energieintensive Unternehmen unter Druck
Ein knappes Zehntel der nötigen Investitionen bis 2045 fällt auf die Industrie - dennoch seien damit hohe Belastungen verbunden, so die Autoren der Studie. Die Investitionen konzentrierten sich auf wenige, besonders energieintensive Unternehmen. "Häufig sind hiermit auch einschneidende Änderungen der Produktionsprozesse und des Geschäftsmodells verbunden. Einzelne Unternehmen müssen sehr hohe Summen in neue Produktionsanlagen investieren."
Viele dieser Unternehmen stünden zudem im internationalen Wettbewerb und könnten höhere Kosten nicht immer über steigende Produktpreise an ihre Kunden weitergeben. Auch die Produktionskosten könnten mit dem Abschied von fossilen Energieträgern wie Kohle und Gas steigen.
Investitionen in den Klimaschutz und entsprechende Technologien kosten aber nicht nur Geld, sie können es auch sparen. "Die Abkehr von fossilen Energieimporten spart Kosten und reduziert Abhängigkeiten", betonen die Autoren.
Andersherum berge der Klimawandel große wirtschaftliche Risiken: So habe etwa die Hitzewelle 2026 die deutsche Wirtschaftsleistung deutlich geschmälert. Die durch Extremwetterereignisse verursachten Vermögensschäden in Deutschland in den vergangenen fünf Jahren werden der Förderbank zufolge auf mehr als 50 Milliarden Euro geschätzt.
gri/pgr (dpa, kna)
description: Um bis 2045 klimaneutral zu werden, müssen in Deutschland einer Studie zufolge sechs Billionen Euro investiert werden. Nach Überzeugung der Autoren lohnen sich die Ausgaben, weil ihnen ein hoher Nutzen gegenübersteht.

title: Зеленський повідомив, що Німеччина організовує зустріч "коаліції охочих"
content_c:
Зеленський повідомив, що Німеччина організовує зустріч "коаліції охочих"
Президент Володимир Зеленський після розмови з канцлером Фрідріхом Мерцом повідомив, що Німеччина працює над організацією зустрічі "коаліції охочих", а також анонсував зустріч радників із нацбезпеки у форматі Е3 – Україна.
Джерело: "Європейська правда" з посиланням на допис Зеленського в Х
Деталі: За його словами, лідери обговорили, як Росія реагує на заяву президента Трампа про енергетичне припинення вогню новими атаками на українські енергооб'єкти.
"Саме так себе поводять росіяни, коли тиск слабшає. Дуже важливо, щоб Європа й далі діяла принципово", – наголосив Зеленський.
"Німеччина працює над організацією зустрічі Коаліції охочих. Так само важливо працювати і в усіх інших форматах, які можуть додати сили Україні та всій Європі", – додав він.
Також вони домовились про зустріч радників із нацбезпеки у форматі Е3 – Україна.
У свою чергу Мерц розповів, що обговорив із Зеленським російські повітряні удари по цивільних об'єктах та українській енергетичній інфраструктурі.
"Росія має погодитися на перемир'я щодо енергетичної інфраструктури – це важливий крок на шляху до тривалого миру в Україні", – наголосив німецький канцлер.
Що передувало:
- Канцлер Німеччини Фрідріх Мерц раніше висловив незгоду з президентом США Дональдом Трампом у зв'язку з угодою з господарем Кремля Володимиром Путіним щодо експорту дизельного палива.
- Президент США Дональд Трамп 9 жовтня заявив, що поспілкувався з правителем Росії Владіміром Путіним та досягнув із ним домовленості про поставки російського дизельного палива на американський та світові ринки.
- Домовленість Трампа і Путіна викликала обурення в Україні та в європейських столицях.

title: Замість дослідів наосліп. Комп’ютерні симуляції допомогли знайти нові способи лікування Альцгеймера
content_c:
Замість дослідів наосліп. Комп’ютерні симуляції допомогли знайти нові способи лікування Альцгеймера
Вчені розкрили спосіб пришвидшити пошук ліків від деменції (Фото: depositphotos.com)
Чи може математика допомогти знайти нові шляхи боротьби з хворобою Альцгеймера?
Шантія Ярахмадіан, доцент кафедри математики та статистики Університету штату Міссісіпі, вивчає вплив таких металів, як мідь та цинк, на поведінку бета-амілоїду. Цей білок здатний склеюватися в токсичні скупчення та формувати бляшки, характерні для хвороби Альцгеймера.
Про це пише Science Daily.
Математичне моделювання дає змогу вченим досліджувати заплутані біологічні взаємодії, описуючи їх за допомогою рівнянь і комп’ютерних симуляцій. Завдяки цьому дослідники можуть перевіряти вплив різних факторів на процес і прогнозувати розвиток подій при зміні певних умов.
Шантія Ярахмадіан пояснив силу математичного підходу для медицини. Вчений зазначив, що «кожне біологічне явище відбувається у фізичному світі, у просторі та часі, і пов’язане зі змінами форми, кількості та матерії. Завдяки абстрактній силі математика дозволяє знаходити закономірності, перевіряти гіпотези та робити прогнози, які неможливо отримати лише шляхом спостережень. Математика не замінює лабораторні чи клінічні дослідження, вона доповнює їх, допомагаючи зрозуміти систему в цілому, визначити найважливіші механізми та спрямувати майбутні експерименти».
Такий підхід може бути особливо корисним для вивчення хвороби Альцгеймера, яка включає безліч паралельних біологічних процесів, складних для ізольованого лабораторного вивчення.
Аби розібратися в механізмі появи небезпечних утворень, Ярахмадіан створив математичну систему, яка відтворює хімічні реакції взаємодії заряджених іонів міді та цинку з білком бета-амілоїдом.
Молекули бета-амілоїду здатні склеюватися між собою в процесі агрегації. З часом ці скупчення перетворюються на бляшки, які вважаються головною патологічною ознакою хвороби Альцгеймера.
Модель детально оцінює, як електрично заряджені іони металів прискорюють накопичення білка. Також вона дозволяє вченим перевірити два потенційні терапевтичні підходи, покликані заблокувати процес цієї небезпечної агрегації.
Замість тривалих спроб виключно в лабораторії, дослідники можуть використовувати симуляції для аналізу реакцій та швидкого пошуку найперспективніших напрямків для практичної перевірки.
Математична модель має реальну цінність лише тоді, коли її прогнози точно відображають справжні експерименти. Для перевірки створеної системи Ярахмадіан разом із колегами зіставив результати комп’ютерних симуляцій із реальними лабораторними вимірюваннями, отриманими за допомогою атомно-силової мікроскопії.
Цей сучасний метод візуалізації використовує надтонкий зонд для вивчення мікроскопічних структур, дозволяючи детально спостерігати за крихітними скупченнями білків та інших органічних матеріалів.
Математична модель повністю відтворила закономірності, зафіксовані в експериментах. Цей збіг доводить, що система правильно схопила важливі особливості злипання білків бета-амілоїду за досліджуваних умов.
Отримані висновки підтверджують, що математичні симуляції здатні допомогти вченим розібратися в причинах утворення білкових згустків і знайти дієві способи вплинути на цей процес. Хоча робота ще не пропонує готових ліків, вона дає надійний компас для подальших лабораторних пошуків.
Правова інформація. Ця стаття містить загальні відомості довідкового характеру і не повинна розглядатися як альтернатива рекомендаціям лікаря. NV не несе відповідальності за будь-який діагноз, поставлений читачем на основі матеріалів сайту. NV також не несе відповідальності за зміст інших інтернет-ресурсів, посилання на які присутні в цій статті. Якщо вас турбує стан вашого здоров’я, зверніться до лікаря.

title: Путін не хоче зупиняти удари по Україні: Кремль відкинув перемир’я і показав справжні наміри
content_c:
Путін не хоче зупиняти удари по Україні: Кремль відкинув перемир’я і показав справжні наміри
Аналітики ISW переконані, що Росія не збирається зупиняти удари по Україні перед зимою.
Високопосадовці агресора Російської Федерації підтвердили, що домовленості про припинення вогню немає. Москва категорично відкидає будь-які пропозиції про перемир’я, які дали б Україні змогу організувати та провести вибори.
Про це йдеться у звіті Інституту вивчення війни (ISW).
Зокрема, міністр закордонних справ Росії Сергій Лавров заявив, що нібито президент України Володимир Зеленський намагається забезпечити припинення вогню для відновлення військових сил. Він нахабно висловився, мовляв, не вірить, що Зеленський «заслужив перепочинок» від війни.
Своєю чергою, речник Кремля Дмитро Пєсков наголосив, що Москва не зацікавлена у пропозиції Зеленського щодо 60-денного припинення вогню, яке дозволило б Києву організувати та провести вибори. З його слів, «фюрер» РФ Володимир Путін готовий наказати про одноденну паузу в ударах, щоб Україна могла провести вибори. Втім, він повторив послідовну відмову Кремля від ширшого припинення вогню.
Аналітики ISW наголошують, що одноденне припинення вогню — несерйозна пропозиція. Ба більше — це фактично є відмовою Кремля від будь-якого припинення вогню, яке дозволить Києву організувати та провести законні вибори.
Окрім того, заявляють аналітики, заяви Кремля у зв’язку з ударом по енергетичній інфраструктурі України 11-12 жовтня підтверджують, що припинення вогню не існує, і що Москва досі відхилила умови запропонованого припинення вогню, про яке Дональд Трамп оголосив 11 жовтня.
«Кремль регулярно відхиляє компромісні пропозиції, які не вигідні Росії в односторонньому порядку, і Росія, ймовірно, відмовиться погодитися на припинення своїх ударів по українській енергетичній інфраструктурі напередодні зими», — йдеться у звіті.
Удари по російських НПЗ
Окрім того, депутат Держдуми та рупар російських ультранаціоналістів підтримав відхилення Росією пропозиції про припинення вогню в енергетиці та відкрито заявив, що нібито удари України по НПЗ не є основною причиною глобального дефіциту дизельного палива. Олексій Журавльов висловився, мовляв, «всі чудово розуміють», що війна на Близькому Сході є основною причиною дефіциту дизпалива. Він привітав рішення Дональда Трампа частково скасувати санкції на експорт пального та назвав значною перемогою для Росії спроби звинуватити українські удари по НПЗ у глобальному дефіциті дизельного пального, хоча вони не є його основною причиною.
Російський мілблогер також висловив думку, що Москва не зацікавлена у припинення вогню в енергетиці, бо згода утриматися від ударів по українських електростанціях «позбавить її одного з головних важелів тиску, якого ми досягли завдяки тривалим ударам», і що російські удари по українських аеродромах та заводах не такі ефективні, як по українських енергетичних об’єктах.
«Цей російський чиновник і мілблогер відкрито пояснюють стратегічне обґрунтування щодо відмови від будь-якої змістовної угоди про припинення вогню, яка не дозволяє РФ максимізувати шкоду, яку вона завдає Україні. Цей дискурс відображає те, як Кремль очікує не менше, ніж повної перемоги в Україні, і не йде на жодні компроміси щодо цієї мети», — підсумували в Інституті.
Мирні переговори — останні новини
Президент США Дональд Трамп зухвало заявив, що російський диктатор Володимир Путін нібито більше зацікавлений у завершенні війни проти України, ніж президент Володимир Зеленський. Він наголошує, що буцімто між Києвом і Москвою є угода про припинення вогню.
Водночас в ISW переконані, що «угода» Трампа про припинення вогню розв’язала Путіну руки на зиму. Наразі жодних домовленостей між Україною та Росією немає, а сам формат ініціативи створює смертельну загрозу для української енергосистеми напередодні зими.
Виднання The Atlantic наголошує, що за останні 72 години Трамп різко змінив підхід до війни, послабивши обмеження на імпорт дизеля з РФ, почав тиснути на Київ через удари по російських НПЗ та дедалі жорсткіше критикувати українське керівництво.
description: Аналітики ISW переконані, що Росія не збирається зупиняти удари по Україні перед зимою.
content:
Путін не хоче зупиняти удари по Україні: Кремль відкинув перемир’я і показав справжні наміри
Аналітики ISW переконані, що Росія не збирається зупиняти удари по Україні перед зимою.
Високопосадовці агресора Російської Федерації підтвердили, що домовленості про припинення вогню немає. Москва категорично відкидає будь-які пропозиції про перемир’я, які дали б Україні змогу організувати та провести вибори.
Про це йдеться у звіті Інституту вивчення війни (ISW).
Зокрема, міністр закордонних справ Росії Сергій Лавров заявив, що нібито президент України Володимир Зеленський намагається забезпечити припинення вогню для відновлення військових сил. Він нахабно висловився, мовляв, не вірить, що Зеленський «заслужив перепочинок» від війни.
Своєю чергою, речник Кремля Дмитро Пєсков наголосив, що Москва не зацікавлена у пропозиції Зеленського щодо 60-денного припинення вогню, яке дозволило б Києву організувати та провести вибори. Аналітики ISW наголошують, що одноденне припинення вогню — несерйозна пропозиція. Ба більше — це фактично є відмовою Кремля від будь-якого припинення вогню, яке дозволить Києву організувати та провести законні вибори.
